blocks.title: Honors — build the equation, don't receive it
blocks.markdown: CPA varies mass (Inv 1.2), varies force (Inv 1.3), and sees that $F = ma$ falls out of the data. Today you do that **and then refuse to stop there.** You're going to derive the joint law yourself, and find the assumption hiding inside it.

## Derive $F = ma$ from two single-variable experiments

From the lab you hold two separate, one-variable claims:

- **Inv 1.3 (vary force, mass fixed):** doubling the force doubled the acceleration. So at constant mass, $a \propto F$.
- **Inv 1.2 (vary mass, force fixed):** doubling the mass halved the acceleration. So at constant force, $a \propto \dfrac{1}{m}$.

Now the honors step CPA skips. Each experiment only changed *one* variable. To put them together into one law, $a \propto \dfrac{F}{m}$, you have to make a claim neither experiment tested directly: that **force and mass act on acceleration independently** — that changing one doesn't secretly change how the other behaves. The combined law is the *simplest* relationship consistent with both lines, not a forced logical deduction. Write it as an equality and you get $a = k\,\dfrac{F}{m}$.

blocks.title: Setting the constant to 1 *defines* the newton
blocks.markdown: That $k$ isn't handed to you by nature — **you choose it.** Physicists set $k = 1$, which collapses the law to $F = ma$. But that choice isn't free: once $k = 1$, the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s² *must* equal exactly 1 force-unit. That force-unit is what we name the **newton**. You didn't just build the equation — by picking the constant, you defined the unit it's measured in.

terms.definition: the SI unit of force; 1 N is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s², the unit fixed by choosing k = 1 in F = ma
the multiplier k that turns a proportionality (a ∝ F/m) into an equation (a = kF/m); its value is a unit choice, not a law of nature
terms.cognate: constante de proporcionalidad / constante de proporcionalidade

blocks.frame: My a-vs-F line and my a-vs-(1/m) line don't have the same slope, but they're both evidence for F = ma because ___. The independence assumption is ___, and I know force and mass act independently because ___.
blocks.prompt: JUSTIFY (homework): Your a-vs-F line and your a-vs-(1/m) line have different slopes. Explain why two single-variable lines can still justify one joint law, F = ma. Then a classmate objects: 'you just *assumed* force and mass act independently — how do you actually know they do?' Answer them honestly. What in the data, or in further experiment, would let you defend that independence?
